coherence.reasons: Both run diagnosis, why not labor, levers, plan, risks, and both tie titles to sized evidence. X's hierarchy is tidy, but its top line is in tension with its own content. It claims the plan 'reaches about 3.0%' while its risk page says the unoffset 2027 wage rise leaves about 2.5%. It sizes promotions as a full return to the 24% share while also holding ValuMart-area stores at today's depth. It builds a FY2026 covenant bridge and an 'H1 FY2026' roadmap although the board meets in February 2027. Y's governing thought (2.9–3.1%, no blanket cut) matches its bridge: the wage step is inside the base case, the stretch lever is named, and the option table, waves, gates and board decisions all use the same numbers. Y's 'initial answer' page tests its own hypothesis, which is slightly odd but logically consistent.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% blanket cut and lead with promotions, shrink, delivery repricing and store exits, which fits the key's preferred answer. Y weighs alternatives much more fully. It compares five options (management draft, the plan, the plan without the three voted exits, the plan plus exiting home delivery, growing e-commerce) with operating income, margin, one-time cost and constraint fit for each. It gives the three-store exit its own payback (about 3.9 years) and defers that vote to a store-by-store review. It nets a traffic-loss penalty against the promotion gain and sets aside $2M for everyday prices near ValuMart. It proposes a targeted labor rebalance with a reversal trigger, which is the key's conditional option handled properly. It adds low/base/high cases, stage gates and contingency levers. X's alternatives are thinner. Its plan reaches 3.0% only by leaving the wage step out, assuming no volume loss from promotion cuts, and assuming shrink falls to 2.3% with no reinvestment or one-time cost. X does offer sensible sequencing (measure transfer at the six lease-expiry stores before the three voted exits) and respects the owners' wish. Y is the more candid about falling just short of 3.0% in the base case.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: labor at 13% of the decline, e-commerce drag of $10.4M, store exits at $6.6M, fee test at $2.5–2.8M, and up to $10M of shrink give-back. X states causation loosely ('shrink rose as stores ran with fewer hours') and rebuts the category team only with 'sales, not profit'. Its $9.9M promotion gain assumes every dollar leaving promotion is rebought at regular price. Its FY2028 total omits the wage step, and it prices the shrink programme at zero cost. Y flags the quartile data as correlation, not proof. It rebuts the category claim with a break-even calculation and the lack of a location control. It reconciles the dollar bridge to the $32.6M fall, decomposes wage versus hours effects, computes per-order economics for collect versus delivered orders, and logs its calculations. Y does introduce more unsupported inputs: the one-time cost allowances, the 1% volume loss, half the wage step recovered in prices, the pro-rata store split and a shaky vendor-funding sizing. Each is labelled as an assumption and carried into the low case. Y's 'low case is above the covenant' line conflates FY2028 with the FY2026 test, but Y is also the one that notices FY2026 is already closing when the board meets.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage hypothesis using the bridge (13% of the decline, hours offsetting about 70% of the wage rise) and the shrink-by-quartile data, and both replace the e-commerce freeze with repricing. X rejects the labor lever entirely for the plan, mentioning only vague 'scheduling gains outside produce and receiving' as a wage offset. Y is more calibrated. It acknowledges wage inflation as real ($16.7M gross effect). It keeps what the evidence supports: a targeted trim in the high-labor stores, where the two best-staffed quartiles differ by only 0.1 pt of shrink, with hours reinvested in the low-labor stores. It also builds the 2027 wage step into the base case. Y explicitly tests and revises its own starting hypothesis too (commercial fixes alone reach only about 2.1%).

overall.reasons: Both documents reach a defensible, bridge-based conclusion and avoid the main traps. Y would serve the CEO better: its plan includes the wage headwind and promotion volume loss, shows a range, compares real alternatives including the version without the board-vote exits, budgets one-time costs against the $25M cap, and gives the board gated decisions with contingencies. X is crisper and its core arithmetic is sound, but its 3.0% headline rests on optimistic, un-netted lever sizes and excludes a risk it sizes at up to $7.3M. Its covenant argument is also built on a FY2026 timeline that does not fit a February 2027 board meeting.
